reason: The two are variant forms of the same Sanskrit word for the Jina; the Pāśupata homonym stays a separate definition on trm:tirthakara.
Both are the mendicant's rainy-season retreat undertaken so as not to harm beings on the roads; the rules and the festivals attached differ.
Both close or crown the rains with a communal act of reconciliation (Jain mutual forgiveness; Buddhist invitation to admonition); not the same rite.

Kundakunda's standpoint of ultimate reality plays the role of the ultimate level (P1) in relation to a conventional level used for teaching; it describes an individual pure soul and does not declare the world unreal, so only an analogy is asserted.
Both are the conventional level through which the ultimate is taught; the Jain standpoint remains a true partial view (naya), not an appearance.
Utt 23 itself explains Pārśva's and Mahāvīra's different rules by the capacities of each era's disciples — a text-internal instance of the stage-of-the-student principle.

Harikeśa's sacrifice of austerity re-reads the Vedic fire-offering as inner discipline, like the Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣadic internalizations; the Jain text rejects the outer sacrifice rather than subordinating it.
Both Jain passages ground brāhmaṇa-hood in conduct or vows; the Gītā's varṇa by guṇa and karma is a comparable move within the Vedic fold. Correspondence only, not identity.

Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma appear in the Jain universal history as baladevas and vāsudevas; the roles are recast (non-violent Rāma liberated, Lakṣmaṇa and Kṛṣṇa in hell), so this is a narrative correspondence, not an equivalence of doctrine.

Kundakunda's two standpoints divide ultimate from conventional description as the two-truths and Advaita level schemes do (P1); Jain sources insist both standpoints are true partial views, not truth and illusion.
Both are the renunciant's settled rains retreat undertaken to avoid harming beings; the rules differ.
Outwardly similar image worship; Jain sources insist the liberated Jina neither receives nor rewards, so worship works by recollection of qualities — a distinction the tradition keeps.
Pilgrimage to sacred places; the Jain tīrthas are the sites of the Tīrthaṅkaras' kalyāṇakas and nirvāṇas.

The Ācārāṅga's graded allowance of robes and Uttarādhyayana 23's explanation by the dispositions of each era adapt the outward sign to capacity; both sects rank the naked mode highest. Digambara and Śvetāmbara objections recorded.

The tradition's own commentators treat Mahāvīra's and Jamāli's statements as true from different standpoints, Jamāli's error being exclusivity; Jamāli remains a nihnava.
Bhikṣu's laukika/lokottara distinction is one of level: opponents affirm life-saving compassion as merit and social good, which he denies only as spiritual dharma. Both sides' objections recorded.
Same images, same scripture; difference of ritual method. The Terāpantha's rejection of attendant deities remains unreconciled.
Uttarādhyayana 23 itself explains the different rules of Pārśva and Mahāvīra by the dispositions of each era's disciples. Digambaras reject the text.

Right faith as entry (B0); the vows and renunciations as ethical foundation (B1); equanimity, holy-day fasting and living like a mendicant as preparatory discipline (B2); the night-long standing meditation as withdrawal (B3).
The lay ladder is entry (B0), ethical foundation (B1) and preparatory discipline (B2); absorption and insight bands belong to the guṇasthānas that follow muni initiation.
